newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Primakov, Cook clash over Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: Primakov, Cook clash over Bosnia.

text.p: Russia and Britain clashed on Monday over a controversial swoop by NATO peacekeepers on two suspected Bosnian Serb war criminals.

Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov complained to visiting British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook that Russia had not been consulted about last Thursday's raid, which he said would not help the fragile peace process in Bosnia.
"I wouldn't want operations of this kind to be repeated because this will not help to improve the situation," Primakov, speaking at a joint news conference with Cook, said.
Cook played down the disagreement, saying Britain and Russia had a lot in common over Bosnia.

But he refused to give an assurance that the operation, in which prominent police chief Simo Drljaca was killed by British troops under the command of NATO's SFOR (Stabilisation Force) international peacekeeping force, would be one of a kind.

"We have given no guarantees that it will not be repeated," Cook said. "If the situation were to arise again we would plainly wish to reserve our right to respond to the requests from the international criminal court and also from any instructions we might receive from SFOR."
Last week's operation was carried out after the International Criminal Tribunal on the Former Yugoslavia handed down sealed, or secret, indictments against a number of suspected war criminals.
But Primakov said the operation, which his ministry condemned last week as a cowboy raid, went beyond the mandate of the peacekeepers. "In our view the mandate does not authorise detention," he said.
With Russia already bruised by NATO's planned eastward enlargement, Primakov complained to Cook that he had not even been consulted about the raid, which outraged Russia's traditional Serb allies.
"As far as stabilising the situation, this operation is counterproductive in our view," Primakov added.

Cook, the first British cabinet minister to visit Moscow since Labour ended 18 years of Conservative rule in a landslide election win on May 1, reassured Primakov that secrecy had prevented a number of allies from being consulted and said no similar operations were being contemplated.

British officials privately acknowledged that the furious Russian reaction could make NATO think twice before trying to seize former Serb leader Radovan Karadzic, who has also been indicted on war crimes.
They said Bosnia only took up the first few minutes of the ministers' talks and did not sour what was a friendly and productive meeting.
"Primakov had plainly set out to come to this meeting to signal a willingness for a fresh start and a warm relationship with the new government of Britain.
"Both of us were quite clear that, although there may be areas of disagreement and friction around, they weren't going to come between us and that objective," Cook said.
Primakov said that Russia's ties with Britain were very important and that Monday's meeting had laid the foundations of a productive relationship.

The two agreed that the first ministerial meeting of the fledgling NATO-Russia partnership council, pencilled in for September, should examine ways of improving military cooperation on international peacekeeping missions.
The council was set up in May to give Russia, worried about NATO's enlargement, a say in the affairs of its former Cold War foe.
